pool.text: The figure shows the graph of a continuous function \(f(x)\) on the interval \([a, d]\). The shaded region represents the definite integral \(\int_{a}^{c} f(x) \, dx\). If the area of the shaded region is 12 square units and the area of the unshaded region between \(x=c\) and \(x=d\) is 5 square units, what is the value of \(\int_{a}^{d} f(x) \, dx\)?
pool.sol:
The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus relates the definite integral of a function to its antiderivative. Geometrically, the definite integral \(\int_{a}^{b} f(x) \, dx\) represents the net signed area between the curve \(f(x)\) and the x-axis from \(x=a\) to \(x=b\). Areas above the x-axis are positive, and areas below the x-axis are negative.

The problem states that the area of the shaded region, representing \(\int_{a}^{c} f(x) \, dx\), is 12 square units. This implies that this region contributes positively to the net signed area.

The area of the unshaded region between \(x=c\) and \(x=d\) is 5 square units. This means that \(\int_{c}^{d} f(x) \, dx = 5\).

We are asked to find \(\int_{a}^{d} f(x) \, dx\). Using the property of definite integrals that \(\int_{a}^{d} f(x) \, dx = \int_{a}^{c} f(x) \, dx + \int_{c}^{d} f(x) \, dx\), we can substitute the given values.

\(\int_{a}^{d} f(x) \, dx = 12 + 5 = 17\).

Therefore, the value of the definite integral from \(a\) to \(d\) is 17.
